title: the claim behind the bread
hookLine: a white dress, a party, a wafer: and the claim the day was about
tomorrow: the most misunderstood room in the building

cards: A white dress or a clip-on tie. Photos on the church steps, a cake after. First Communion is easy to remember.
What the day was actually about can be fuzzier: in surveys, a lot of Catholics describe the bread as a symbol.

If it was never spelled out for you, you're not behind: First Communion usually comes at about seven, and that's a lot to hold at seven. The Church's own claim is much bigger than a symbol. So here it is, once, plainly.

teach.b: It starts the night before Jesus died, at a Passover meal. He takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and says, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me."

Gave thanks, in Greek, is where the word comes from: eucharistia, thanksgiving. Now the claim. Catholics believe that when the priest says those words at Mass, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ.
They still look, taste and feel like bread and wine. What they are, underneath, has changed. Not a symbol of him: him.
The Church calls it the real presence. In John's Gospel, Jesus calls himself the living bread, and many followers find that too hard and walk away. He lets them go.

After Mass, the consecrated bread that's left is kept in a small box near the altar, the tabernacle, with a red lamp burning beside it. That's why people bend a knee when they walk into an empty church.
They believe he's there. Christians differ here. Orthodox Christians and Lutherans also speak of a real presence; many other Protestants see the meal as a memorial and a sign.

how: Catholics receive the Eucharist at Mass, genuflect toward the tabernacle when entering a church, and many spend quiet time in prayer before it, a practice called adoration.

games.q: Jesus says he is the living bread, and many followers find it too hard and start leaving. what does he do?
o: calls them back and says it's only a metaphor.
games.why: John says many walked away, and Jesus let them go. Catholics see that as a sign he meant it.

practice: One breath with the bell. Think of a time someone simply stayed with you: in a waiting room, on the end of your bed, on the phone. They didn't fix anything.
Breathe in, remembering it. Breathe out slowly.

wordCard.voice: The Eucharist. Thanksgiving: the bread and wine Catholics believe become Christ himself, his real presence. Second word.

orig.note: Greek: thanksgiving. at the Last Supper, Jesus took bread and gave thanks.

carryVoice: Your line: he stayed. It's what the red lamp is saying, in an empty church on a Tuesday afternoon. Day two, done.
